general.oracion_todos_los_dias:
Most gracious God of infinite charity, who have loved all mankind so greatly that You gave us in Your Son the greatest pledge of Your love, that, made man in the womb of a Virgin, He might be born in a manger for our salvation and healing; I, on behalf of all mortals, give You infinite thanks for so great a gift. In return, I offer You the poverty, humility, and other virtues of Your incarnate Son, beseeching You, through His divine merits, the hardships of His birth, and the tender tears He shed in the manger, to prepare our hearts with deep humility, burning love, and complete detachment from all earthly things, so that my newborn Jesus may find in them His cradle and dwell there forever. Amen.

(Pray the Glory Be three times)
general.oracion_virgen_maria:
Sovereign Mary, who, by your great virtues, and especially by your humility, merited that God Himself should become man in your sacred womb, I give infinite thanks to that same Lord for choosing you to be His Mother and, for so high a dignity, adorning you with countless gifts of nature and grace. I beseech you, my Lady, to obtain for us an ardent desire to see the beautiful Child and heroic virtues with which to receive Him into our souls. Obtain this for us through the love with which you brought forth the fruit of your womb, and through the sweet tenderness your soul experienced as you held Him in your arms, pressed Him to your breast, kissed His divine face, and adored Him as your God and your Son. Amen.

(Pray nine Hail Marys in memory of the nine months the Divine Queen carried the Son of God in her most pure womb)
general.oracion_san_jose:
O Most Holy Joseph, husband of Mary and foster father of Jesus! I give infinite thanks to God for choosing you for so high a calling and adorning you with all the gifts befitting so excellent a dignity. I beg you, by the love you bore the Divine Child, to fill my heart with a fervent desire to see Him and receive Him in the Holy Eucharist, until I may see Him and enjoy Him in His divine essence in heaven. Amen.

(Pray one Our Father, one Hail Mary, and one Glory Be)
general.oracion_niño_jesus:
Remember, O most sweet Child Jesus, that You said to the Venerable Margaret of the Blessed Sacrament, and through her to all Your devotees, these words so comforting to our poor, burdened, and suffering humanity:

“Whatever you wish to ask, ask it through the merits of my childhood, and nothing will be denied you.”

Full of confidence in You, O Jesus, who are the very Truth, we come to lay before You all our misery. Help us to lead a holy life, that we may attain a blessed eternity. Grant us, through the infinite merits of Your Incarnation and childhood, the grace of which we are so much in need. We surrender ourselves to You, O omnipotent Child, confident that our hope will not be disappointed and that, by virtue of Your divine promise, You will graciously hear and grant our prayer. Amen.

(Pray the Prayer to the Divine Child three times)

dias.reflexion:
In the beginning, the Word rested in the bosom of His Father in the highest heavens. There He was the cause and the model of all creation. In the depths of an immeasurable eternity, the Child of Bethlehem dwelt before He deigned to descend to earth and visibly take possession of the grotto of Bethlehem.

There is where we must seek His beginning, which never began; there we must trace the genealogy of the Eternal One, who has no ancestors, and contemplate the life of infinite delight that He enjoyed there.

The life of the Eternal Word in the bosom of His Father was a wondrous life. And yet, what a sublime mystery! He sought another dwelling, a created home. It was not because anything was lacking in His eternal dwelling or in His infinite happiness, but because His boundless mercy longed for the redemption and salvation of the human race, which could not be accomplished without Him.

Adam's sin had offended God, and such an infinite offense could only be atoned for by the merits of God Himself. The descendants of Adam had disobeyed and deserved eternal punishment. Therefore, in order to save them and make satisfaction for their guilt, God, without leaving heaven, chose to take the form of man upon earth and, through obedience to the will of His Father, make reparation for that disobedience, ingratitude, and rebellion.

In the designs of His love, He chose to take upon Himself the form, weaknesses, and limitations of humanity; to grow in order to give us spiritual growth; to suffer in order to teach us to die to our passions and our pride.

And so the Eternal Word, burning with the desire to save humanity, resolved to become man Himself and thus redeem the guilty.

The Eternal Word was about to take upon Himself a created nature in the holy house of Nazareth, where Mary and Joseph lived. When the shadow of the divine mystery came upon her, Mary was alone, immersed in prayer. She spent the silent hours of the night in the closest union with God, and while she prayed, the Word took possession of His created dwelling.

Yet He did not come unexpectedly. Before appearing, He sent a messenger: the Archangel Gabriel, who came to ask Mary, on God's behalf, for her consent to the Incarnation. The Creator did not wish to accomplish this great mystery without the consent of His creature.

That moment was most solemn. Mary was free to refuse. With what heavenly delight and ineffable joy must the Most Holy Trinity have awaited Mary's answer—the answer that would be a sweet melody to divine ears, and through which her profound humility would unite itself to the almighty will of God!

The Immaculate Virgin gave her consent. The Archangel disappeared. God clothed Himself in a created nature. The eternal will was fulfilled, and creation reached its completion.

The Word became flesh. Though still invisible to the world, He already dwelt among the people whom His immense love had come to redeem.

Thus began the incarnate life of the Child Jesus. Let us contemplate the glorious soul and the holy body He had taken, and let us adore them deeply.

First, let us contemplate the soul of the Divine Child. In it we find the fullness of sanctifying grace and the beatific knowledge by which, from the very first moment of His life, He saw the divine essence more clearly than all the angels and knew the past and the future with all their hidden mysteries.

He did not acquire through learning anything that He did not already possess through divine infusion from the very first moment of His existence. Yet He willingly took upon Himself all the conditions and weaknesses of our human nature to which He could fittingly submit, even though they were not necessary for the great work He had come to accomplish.

Let us now turn from the soul of the Child Jesus to His body, which was a world of wonders, a masterpiece of God's hands. He chose it to be small and weak like that of every child and subject to all the discomforts of infancy, so that He might become more like us and share in our humiliations.

The beauty of the Divine Child's body was greater than anything ever imagined. And the divine blood that began to flow through His veins from the moment of the Incarnation is the blood that washes away the stains of the sinful world.

Let us ask Him to wash away our own stains in the Sacrament of Reconciliation, so that on the day of His blessed Nativity He may find us purified, forgiven, and ready to receive Him with love and spiritual fruitfulness.

From His mother's womb, the Child Jesus began to practice His complete submission to God, which continued without interruption throughout His entire life.

He adored His Eternal Father, loved Him, submitted Himself to His will, and accepted with resignation the condition in which He found Himself, knowing all its weakness, humiliation, and discomfort.

Who among us would willingly return to such a state while possessing the full use of reason and reflection? Who could knowingly endure such a prolonged and painful martyrdom?

This is where the Divine Child began His painful and humble journey. There He began to humble Himself before His Father, to teach us what God deserves from His creatures, to make reparation for our pride—the source of all our sins—and to make us understand the seriousness and disorder caused by pride.

Do we wish to learn how to pray truly? Let us begin by forming an accurate understanding of prayer, contemplating the Child in His mother's womb.

The Divine Child prays, and He prays in the most perfect way. He does not speak, meditate, or express Himself through tender emotions. His very condition, accepted with the intention of honoring God, is His prayer. And that condition declares most profoundly what God deserves and how He desires to be worshiped by us.

Let us unite ourselves to the prayers of the Child Jesus in Mary's womb. Let us unite ourselves to His profound humility, and let this be the first offering of our sacrifice to God.

Let us give ourselves to God—not to become something, as our vanity constantly desires, but to become nothing; to remain forever surrendered and humbled before Him; to renounce our desire for recognition, our concern for greatness, even spiritual greatness, and every movement of vanity.

Let us disappear from our own sight, so that God alone may be everything for us.

We have already contemplated the life that the Child Jesus lived in the womb of His most pure Mother. Today, let us contemplate the life that Mary herself lived during this same period.

We must consider her if we wish to understand, as far as our limited human capacity allows, the sublime mysteries of the Incarnation and the way in which we should respond to them.

Mary never ceased longing for the moment when she would enjoy the earthly vision of God incarnate—the face of God made man.

She was about to see that human face which would illuminate heaven throughout all eternity. She was about to read filial love in those very eyes whose rays would forever spread happiness among millions of the elect.

What must have been the thoughts of the Blessed Virgin during those days of waiting! What profound recollection, what tender love, what humility and adoration must have filled her soul as she awaited the birth of her Divine Son.

Let us unite ourselves to Mary's expectation. Let us ask her to teach us how to wait for Jesus with faith, silence, love, and profound humility, so that our hearts may be prepared to receive Him.

Jesus had been conceived in Nazareth, the home of Joseph and Mary, and according to every human expectation, it would seem that He should be born there.

But God had arranged otherwise. The prophets had foretold that the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem of Judea, the city of David.

In order for this prophecy to be fulfilled, God made use of something that seemed to have no connection with this purpose: the decree issued by the Emperor Augustus ordering all the subjects of the Roman Empire to register in the place from which their families originated.

Mary and Joseph, being descendants of David, were not exempt from going to Bethlehem. Neither the condition of the Blessed Virgin nor Joseph's need to continue his daily work, upon which their livelihood depended, could spare them from this long and difficult journey during the harshest and most uncomfortable season of the year.

Jesus knew the place where He was to be born, and He inspired His parents to surrender themselves to Divine Providence. In this way, without fully realizing it, they participated in the fulfillment of God's designs.

Let us learn from them to trust in Providence, even when God's plans appear difficult, unexpected, or contrary to our own expectations.

The Child Jesus knows the path that leads us to Him. Let us trust Him and allow Him to guide our lives according to His divine will.

Let us picture the journey of Mary and Joseph toward Bethlehem, carrying with them the Creator of the universe made man, still hidden in Mary's womb.

Let us contemplate the humanity and obedience of this Divine Child. Although He belonged to the Jewish people and had loved His people for centuries with an inexplicable predilection, He now obeyed a foreign ruler who ordered a census of his province, as though there were something attractive in this circumstance and He wished to take advantage of the opportunity to be officially registered as a subject at the very moment He was coming into the world.

Is it not strange that the humiliation which causes such invincible repugnance in human beings should appear to be the one created thing that attracts the Creator?

Does not the humility of Jesus teach us to love this beautiful virtue?

Oh, may the moment soon arrive when the Desired One of the Nations appears! Everything longs for this blessed event.

The world, immersed in darkness and suffering, searching everywhere and finding no relief from its troubles, sighs for its Redeemer.

The longing of Joseph and the expectation of Mary are beyond the power of human language to express.

The Eternal Father, if we may dare use such a human expression, seems lovingly eager to give His only Son to the world and to see Him take His place among visible creatures.

The Holy Spirit burns with the desire to bring into the light of day that holy humanity which He Himself has formed with such divine care.

And as for the Divine Child, the object of so many longings, let us remember that He is coming toward us just as He is coming toward Bethlehem.

Let us hasten His coming through our desire. Let us purify our souls so that they may become His mystical dwelling, and our hearts His earthly home.

May our acts of mortification and detachment “prepare the way of the Lord and make His paths straight.”

Joseph and Mary arrive in Bethlehem seeking lodging, but they cannot find any. Either every place is already occupied, or they are turned away because of their poverty.

Yet nothing can disturb the interior peace of those who are firmly rooted in God.

If Joseph felt sadness as he was rejected from house to house, thinking of Mary and the Child, he would also smile with holy tranquility whenever he looked upon his chaste wife.

The Child, still unborn, rejoiced at these refusals, for they were the prelude to the humiliations He would soon endure.

Every harsh voice and every door that closed before them was like a sweet melody to His ears. This was what He had come to seek. The desire for these humiliations had helped move Him to take human form.

O Divine Child of Bethlehem! While so many people spend these days in celebrations and amusements, or resting comfortably in rich and splendid homes, Your parents have endured days of fatigue and every kind of humiliation.

Oh, the spirit of Bethlehem is the spirit of a world that has forgotten God!

How often has it also been our spirit?

Do we not continually close the door through our ignorance to God's invitations, when He calls us to conversion, holiness, or conformity to His will?

Do we not misuse our sufferings, failing to recognize their heavenly character, even though each one bears within it a message from God?

God comes to us many times throughout our lives, but we do not recognize His face. We recognize Him only when He turns away and leaves after we have rejected Him.

The sun sets on December 24 behind the rooftops of Bethlehem, and its final rays gild the tops of the rugged hills surrounding the town.

Rough men push rudely against the Lord in the streets of that eastern village and close their doors when they see His Mother.

The vault of heaven glows above the hills frequented by the shepherds. One by one, the stars begin to appear.

Only a few hours remain, and the Eternal Word will appear.

Night has completely fallen over the countryside of Bethlehem.

Rejected by men and finding no shelter, Mary and Joseph have left the inhospitable town and taken refuge in a grotto at the foot of the hill.

Following the Queen of Angels was the donkey that had humbly carried her throughout the journey. In the cave they found a gentle ox, probably left there by one of the travelers who had gone into the city seeking lodging.

The Divine Child, unknown to His rational creatures, would now have to turn to the animals to warm the cold atmosphere of that winter night with their gentle breath and, through their humble presence, offer the respect and adoration that Bethlehem had denied Him.

The reddish light of Joseph's lantern faintly illuminates that poorest of places—a manger filled with straw, a prophetic image of the wonders of the altar and of the intimate and miraculous Eucharistic union that Jesus would one day establish with humanity.

Mary remains in adoration in the midst of the grotto, and the hours of this mysterious night pass silently.

But midnight has arrived.

And suddenly, within the manger that had been empty only moments before, we see the Divine Child.

He is there.

The Eternal Word has become flesh.

The One whom heaven cannot contain now lies in a manger.

The King of Heaven has come to us in poverty and humility.

Let us adore Him.

Let us welcome Him into our hearts.

Let us offer Him the love, tenderness, and devotion that the world failed to give Him that holy night.

O Divine Child Jesus, come into our hearts and make them Your dwelling place.

May our souls become Your Bethlehem, our hearts Your manger, and our lives a continual offering of love to You.

gozos.texto:
O Wisdom Most High of the sovereign God, You who humbly lower Yourself to a child's reach!
O Divine Child, come and teach us the wisdom that makes us truly wise!
Come to our souls!
Come, do not delay!

O mighty Adonai, You who spoke to Moses and gave the commandments to the people of Israel!
Come quickly to rescue us, and let a weak child show forth a mighty arm!
Come to our souls!
Come, do not delay!

O sacred Root of Jesse, You who from on high present to the world Your fragrant spikenard!
Sweetest Child, who has been called the Lily of the Valleys, the beautiful flower of the field.
Come to our souls!
Come, do not delay!

O Key of David, that opens for the exile the closed doors of the royal palace!
Draw us out, O Child, with Your gentle hand, from the sad prison that sin has forged!
Come to our souls!
Come, do not delay!

O Light of the East, sun of eternal rays, let us see Your splendor amid the darkness!
Child so precious, joy of the Christian, let the smile shine forth from Your sweet lips.
Come to our souls!
Come, do not delay!

Spotless Mirror, Holy of Holies, unequaled image of the sovereign God!
Blot out our faults, save the exile, and in the form of a child, give shelter to the wretched!
Come to our souls!
Come, do not delay!

King of nations, glorious Emmanuel, longing of Israel, Shepherd of the flock!
Child who shepherds with a gentle staff both the wild sheep and the meek lamb!
Come to our souls!
Come, do not delay!

Let the heavens open and let beneficent dew rain down from above like holy watering!
Come, beautiful Child, come, God made man! Shine forth, star of God! Spring up, flower of the field!
Come to our souls!
Come, do not delay!

Come, for Mary already prepares her arms to hold her Child in the days now near!
Come, for Joseph, with sacred longing, is preparing to become the shrine of Your holy love!
Come to our souls!
Come, do not delay!

Help of the weak, refuge of the suffering, comfort of the sorrowful, light of the exile!
Life of my life, my beloved Lord, my constant friend, my divine Brother!
Come to our souls!
Come, do not delay!

Come before my eyes, which are enamored of You! Let me kiss Your feet! Let me kiss Your hands!
Prostrate on the ground, I stretch out my arms to You, and more than my words, my weeping speaks to You!
Come to our souls!
Come, do not delay!

Come, our Savior, for whom we sigh!
Come to our souls, come, do not delay!
